item.title: UN says we’re going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a “now what?” answer
item.description:
Best case is now an overshoot to 1.8º C, accompanied by massive carbon removal.

In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit.

On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP)acknowledged that realityand conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out.

Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we’ve gone over it no matter which records you choose.

The UN relies on temperatures averaged over a few decades to determine where we are, which means we have technically not gone above the limit yet. But, as temperatures seem stubbornly disinterested in dropping much even after extremely hot years, we’re likely at the start of the period where the 1.5° goal is passed. So, while it’s not technically too late to get on a pathway that keeps us below this, practically it’s already too late.

UNEP’s acknowledgment of this reality is straightforward, albeit couched in a bit of optimism. “Decades of insufficient climate action makes exceedance of 1.5° C unavoidable,” its latest report states. “Whether it will be temporary crucially depends on decisions taken today.” In other words, we might be committed to exceeding the goal, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that we’re accepting that global temperatures will need to stay above the 1.5° C mark.

The Paris Agreement’s means of getting to that goal was to have its signatories set emissions-reduction targets and then progressively expand those as policy tools and technology matured. Progress would be measured at key points through a “stocktake” process. But not a lot of countries followed up on what they agreed to. “While the year 2030 is drawing closer, collectively countries have still not aligned policies with [agreed to] targets,” UNEP concedes. In fact, the gap between targets and actual policy would look even worse if the US were still part of the process, instead of seeing the Trump administration pull out of the agreement a second time.

A decade into the process, the needed tightening of policies has also been insufficient. In its new analysis, UNEP highlights that existing policies would likely leave us at 2.8° C above preindustrial temperatures by the end of the century, while even the stretch goals under the Paris Agreement would drop that by just 0.2°. Many countries have set net-zero goals outside of the Paris Framework, but including all of those would still leave us at 2.1° C above preindustrial temperatures by the century’s end. In all of these scenarios, temperatures would continue to rise in the ensuing century.

And we don’t seem to be closer to getting our act together. Emissions were largely flat between 2024 and 2025 (there appears to be a slight decline, but within uncertainties of zero change), and emissions from burning fossil fuels were actually up, offset by better land-use management. But to have reached any significant goals, they needed to be dropping by now.

But UNEP is a rare organization, in that it’s willing to say the worst is not necessarily yet to come. “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5° C raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts,” the report says. “The task now, therefore, is not only to ensure that global warming stays well below 2°C, but to minimize the duration and magnitude of overshoot and establish a credible return path to 1.5° C by the end of the century.”

The scenario it lays out has a 66 percent chance of keeping warming to a maximum of 1.8° C above preindustrial temperatures, and to have even odds that we can have temperatures back down below 1.5° by the century’s end.

The first thing that should be obvious is that this would require removing some of the emissions we are presently placing in the atmosphere. For a technology that is still in its infancy, the goals seem extreme: 320 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide pulled out of the atmosphere by the century’s end. At the same time, that’s the rough equivalent of just over five years of present emissions pulled out over decades.

But that also has to be accompanied by major emissions cuts and a transition away from fossil fuels. UNEP’s scenario would cut coal use for electricity generation by 75 percent by 2035, and phase out the fuel by 2040. All uses of oil and gas would need to be cut by 30 and 35 percent, respectively, by 2040. This is needed because greenhouse gas emissions would have to drop by 70 percent between now and 2040.

Again, this highlights the insufficiency of current climate pledges. UNEP determined that these would only cut emissions by about 12 percent by 2035. Put differently, by 2035, current pledges would leave us emitting 16 gigatonnes more carbon dioxide in 2035 than we would need to stay on the minimal overshoot pathway. (The gap between pledges and needs is notably smaller in the scenario that would keep warming to 2° C by century’s end, which involves a 5 gigatonne difference.)

There are failures across the board here. While coal use is declining, it’s not projected to fall nearly fast enough over the next decade. Oil and gas need to start falling, but they’re projected to rise for a decade or more. (This report would have been in preparation before the conflict with Iran disrupted oil and gas supplies, and the data on any conservation and electrification driven by shortages is not available yet.) Solar and wind are growing fast enough for a scenario that includes reasonable conservation and efficiency efforts, but because demand is rising so quickly, they’re falling behind where we need them as a percentage of the electrical grid.

The report suggests we can still limit the impact of failing to meet our climate goals. But doing so will require major efforts from many countries—the same countries that got us here by not taking the initial goals seriously enough.

item.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
item.description:
For 3 days this month, 333 exit nodes were hacked in hopes of stealing sensitive data.

Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.

The hijacking began in late August, when,according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installedEbury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.

Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.

Ultimately, 333 exit relays were involved in the SSH and email interception campaign, although investigators haven’t established how the attackers gained control of all the underlying servers. The attackers then reconfigured the servers. One set of changes redirected SSH traffic traversing Tor to one of 12 attacker-controlled interceptor servers. Tor users who ignored warnings that the SSH host key had changed would then enter their SSH passwords.

A second set of changes caused the exit nodes to block ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995—used to accept various forms of encrypted email—while continuing to allow ports for receiving unencrypted email. If email services downgraded the connections, the attackers used their access to the exit nodes to obtain unencrypted messages. It’s unclear whether any such downgrade attempts succeeded. The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5.

Tor volunteers partially outlined the initial compromise of the management server and Switzerland2 and the attempt to intercept unencrypted email.Tuesday’s reportrevealed many new details, including how many exit nodes were compromised and how the attackers used them to redirect SSH traffic.

“If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won’t notice anything at first,” Kaba, the name of the Tor volunteer who authored the post, wrote. “Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you’re unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers. That’s exactly what happened to me on Friday morning.” Kaba then received the following warning:

@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@ WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!Someone could be eavesdropping on you right now (man-in-the-middle attack)!It is also possible that a host key has just been changed.The fingerprint for the ED25519 key sent by the remote host isSHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E.Please contact your system administrator.

The volunteer investigated further and found that when people ignored the warning, the attacker (1) stole the SSH password, (2) opened a connection to the server and observed all typed commands, and (3) opened a second connection and infected the server with Ebury.

To investigate the campaign, Kaba created a script that polled all of Tor’s roughly 3,000 exit nodes to check whether they received a correct SSH fingerprint from a test server. The test server then checked whether the connection came from a pinned exit node or one of 12 SSH interception servers used by the attacker. The volunteer further set up a honeypot to observe the interception software attempting to log in and install Ebury.

Several mysteries remain. Tor volunteers still don’t know how the attackers accessed so many servers. One possibility is that a company hosting them was hacked, but the theory is inconclusive. Another open question is who is behind the attack. “The use of Ebury and the broad collection of unencrypted data point to a financially motivated crime group,” Kaba wrote. “Though this too is just speculation.”

A last perplexing finding: why did Switzerland2 accept an RSA key when there’s no evidence it was an authorized SSH certificate?

The takeaway from the event is the crucial role in-depth defense plays in preventing data theft in mass hacks like this one. Those measures include configuring email accounts to accept only encrypted traffic and reject unencrypted ports. Another is to disable password authentication in favor of SSH keys.

item.title: Forget “Malaise 2.0,” GM says it’s still all-in on EVs and autonomy
item.description:
General Motors’ plans will require quite a lot of customers’ trust.

It’s easy to criticize US automakers and their tepid approach to electric vehicles under the current administration and the expiration of theEV tax credit. It’s also easy to look at the rest of the world’s embrace of EVs and wonder if the US is entering a “Malaise 2.0” era. Which is why GM wants the world to know that it is still focused on its end goals of electrification, autonomy, and improving vehicle quality while reducing development time.

At this year’s GM Forward event, company executives announced that its hands-off, eyes-off Super Cruise technology will expand across the lineup and be available on nearly every vehicle. This will include the pickup trucks and the crossovers, and not just the Escalade IQ that it was announced for last year.

Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, said the company is testing this technology to the tune of 1 million miles (1.6 million km) a month in both the virtual and real world. The goal is that not only would the vehicle be able to take you places, but it could go and do things for you.

That sounds rather dystopian. But Anderson told Ars in an interview that once you realize what your vehicle is capable of doing (beyond the paradigm of being a car to go places), it opens up a world of convenience that might be hard to envision right now. He’s not talking about an Optimus-style robot that’ll do your laundry, but a tool that you use every day that expands to do more things.

GM’s newly announced OnStar AI will play a role. “Imagine you worked late, and you get in your car to go home,” he told us. “Your car might remember that you ordered takeout from a restaurant recently that you frequent and like. The car could prompt you and place a pick-up order for you, which will be ready when you arrive to pick it up.”

Trust is the key here, and Anderson reiterated that several times, suggesting that a car might be a more trusted piece of technology than a mobile phone. “People have a relationship with their cars that they don’t have with other things,” he said. “If your phone randomly suggested your favorite restaurant, it might give you pause, but if your car did so within the appropriate context you might be more willing to accept that.”

OnStar AI will do more than just learn your habits; it will be able to help you better understand and better use your vehicle, we’re told. For example: a driver hears the car beep but doesn’t know what the alert was for. In this case, they could ask OnStar and it would be able to tell them—for example, a speed limit warning. Being a specialized AI trained specifically on the details of the car, it can be integrated in a way that other models, like Google’s Gemini, cannot.

Thanks to new compute on board, announced at last year’sForward, the car will be able to handle much of that processing locally without requiring a connection to the cloud at all. But a cloud connection could improve the drive or make it safer. For some time now, automakers and suppliers have promised systems that crowdsource data to infer and predict road conditions—if you’re driving through a snowy area, and the cars in front of you have had traction control events, you could receive a warning to be extra careful as you approach.

GM also wants to keep customers within its own ecosystem. Imagine a two-car, two-GM OnStar AI household, and you’re late picking up your child from practice. Here, OnStar AI could look and see your spouse is actually closer, swap roles, and re-direct you to the takeout place to pick up dinner. OK, it’s a very specific use case.

Trust continues to be the key. Anderson knows that must be earned, and trust is difficult to get back if it’s broken.

His approach is to put that customer trust first in what he does. For example, GM’s new infotainment system will have the ability to record from the cameras as a dash cam and store that video. And it can upload that video to GM’s cloud to access anywhere. But it is end-to-end encrypted, meaning that when it hits GM’s servers it’s in a format that GM can’t read. If law enforcement wanted to view the video, GM wouldn’t be able to help because it could not decrypt the video.

That is the type of trust that is absolutely needed when dealing with this type of personal data, because there is a convenience to a lot of this. But the opportunity for that data to be misused is also there—it wasn’ttoo long ago that GM was found to be selling customers’ data, often without their knowledge, to insurance companies.

We’ll want to experience GM’s new attitude in practice, of course, but hearing an automotive executive directly address that concern head-on was refreshing.

This all leads into the fully autonomous functionality that GM is working on. Ars also spoke with Rashed Haq, VP of Autonomous Vehicles at GM, about the current state of the level 4 technology, and more importantly, when it’ll be safe enough for customers to use.

“We look at two key factors, safety and roadcraft,” Haq told me.

Safety obviously includes the vehicle’s occupants, but also the general public. And that requires millions of miles of testing in the real world butalso digitally. Automakers like GM will never be able to prepare for every scenario, but it will combine training data with an open vocabulary to assess what information is there and make a driving decision based on that. Haq also reiterated the company’s expectation that when the car is driven by the computer, the responsibility falls on GM and the computer if something goes wrong due to a malfunction.

The second key here is roadcraft. That means making sure that the vehicle isn’t creating a hazard or problem for other vehicles on the road. You’ve likely seen videos where Waymo vehicles are all crowded on a streetblocking traffic: That’s not something GM wants its cars to do.

Eventually, all of this leads back to the idea of a car working for you for tasks that aren’t just driving places. Your car could go pick up your dry cleaning, or at least drive there and wait while someone comes out and deposits the clothes inside it. You could ride to school with a child, both sitting in the back seat, reclaiming some time together because the car is doing the mundane task of driving.

It’s an interesting idea and will only happen if consumers trust GM and their vehicle enough to do that, something we won’t know until closer to that technology maturing.

GM also announced its Gen-4 EV architecture based on LMR battery technology.As we learned last year, the new lithium manganese-rich battery chemistry promises energy densities close to nickel-manganese-cobalt but without that expensive cobalt, making their cost closer to that of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry cells.

A 30 percent cheaper battery should help GM offer a wide variety of EVs, hopefully including some affordable models, like the now-limited-run Bolt.

If GM can also deliver affordable autonomy, built on a foundation of trust and safety, it’ll be a unique offering from a US automaker and will put the company in a better position to take on the challenges from global competition.

item.title: Sauron recruits his future Ringwraiths in Rings of Power S3 trailer
item.description:
“I will take my place as the conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.”

Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Powerreturns next month for its third season. Prime Videounveiled a teaserearlier this year at San Diego Comic-Con, but we haven’t heard much about the new season otherwise. We now have the official full trailer, and it’s jam-packed with a rising Sauron, who is intent on conquering Middle-Earth with his army of Orcs—with the fractured opposition of elves, dwarves, and men scrambling to figure out how best to stop him. We also meet the human men who will become the Ringwraiths; the showrunners have dubbed them the Nazgnagol (“Rings-servant”).

(Some spoilers for the first two seasons below.)

Prime Videomade a majorinvestment inThe Rings of Powerwhen it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. S3 is set seven years after the events of S2 and opens when the war between the elves and Sauron is at its height. Per the official synopsis:

In season three, Middle-earth is at war. Five years have passed since the fall of Eregion. Sauron’s armies have marched across the whole of the world, conquering all in their path. Only a few isolated pockets stand between the Dark Lord and total victory—Khazad-dǔm, where the Dwarves are now sealed deep within their mountain halls, and the elven realms of Lindon and Rivendell, which are protected by their Three Rings.

But deep in the land of Mordor, in his newly completed tower of Barad-dûr, the Dark Lord toils day and night, obsessed with harnessing a power that will bring the last of his enemies to their knees:One ring to rule them all.Now, all the free peoples of Middle-earth—Dwarves, Elves, Men, and Wizards alike—must find a way to come together, in a race against time to prevent Sauron from achieving his goal of utter domination of all life

We’re also getting some new characters this season, most notably Jamie Campbell Bower as Galadriel’s (Morfydd Clark) long-lost husband, Celeborn. Zubin Varla will play Khamul the Easterling of Rhun; Eddie Marsan will play Thrain, older brother to King Durin IV (Owain Arthur); Andrew Richardson will play Anarion, youngest son of Elendil (Lloyd Owen) and brother to Isildur (Maxim Baldry); and Adam Young will play an Orc named Marnukh, who “might not be what he seems.” Oh, and none other than Simon Pegg will voice the fiery Balrog.

The first four episodes ofThe Rings of PowerS3 premiere on November 11, 2026, on Prime Video. The fifth and sixth episodes will be available on November 18, and the final two episodes will premiere on November 25, 2026.

item.title: Hackers got a four-day head start on epic PHP2Shell vulnerability
item.description:
Hackers were already probing the bug before defenders were told it existed.

Amazon has warned thatvulnerabilities in a programming languagethat underpins much of the Internet, discovered using AI tools, are being “broadly exploited” as governments and companies rush to secure their systems.

The world’s largest cloud computing provider on Wednesday said it had identified an attempt by hackers to exploit the bug four days before the weakness was disclosed to the public.

Amazon added the flaws were “now being broadly exploited in the wild.”

The US National Security Agency and UK authorities earlier on Wednesday warned that the vulnerabilities had left websites around the world critically exposed to hacking, as some governments in Europe were reportedly taking sites offline while they patched the two security flaws.

The vast impact of the bugs, uncovered with the help of OpenAI and Google models after being undetected for more than a decade, highlights the ability of AI to upend cybersecurity.

The release of new models earlier this year from Anthropic and OpenAI with powerful cyber capabilities prompted warnings from politicians and financial regulators and led the US government to temporarily limit their rollout.

The NSA on Wednesday warned all organizations using the programming language known as PHP to immediately update their systems or take them offline.

The developers responsible for maintaining PHP released software updates to patch the vulnerabilities earlier on Wednesday.

“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the NSA said. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”

Researchers at two US cybersecurity groups, Calif and Wiz, discovered the vulnerabilities. Alphabet-owned Wiz estimated that the compromised programming language powered about 70 percent of all websites in the world.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said on Wednesday. “To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.”

“It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with Internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” the AI lab added.

OpenAI worked with PHP, Calif, and Wiz to verify the vulnerabilities and develop the patches.

The White House said federal agencies were assessing the potential impacts of the bugs on government systems and critical infrastructure.

PHP’s wide presence on the Internet is largely because WordPress, the most widely used website-building platform, is written primarily in PHP and relies on it to function.

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said the vulnerabilities could potentially allow a hacker to take control of a website’s server without needing a password or other login credentials. “The NCSC is encouraging UK organizations to take immediate action,” it said.

item.title: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display
item.description:
Tile-based color palettes go way beyond the four shades of red on original hardware.

Last year, wereported on Red Viper, a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash ofSuper Game Boy-style colorto Nintendo’s famously failed red-on-black “portable” 3D headset from the ’90s. Now, a new emulation experiment,VBoy Color, has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame.

Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy’s four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color’sreadme filesexplain how the emulator’s game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8×8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall inMario Clash, for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game.

The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games likeJack Bros.orVertical Force, where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements.

VBoy Color comes with built-in color packs for 15 different games, which actually represents a significant chunk of the Virtual Boy’s limited official library. Tinkerers can edit those packs manually using built-in video tools to color individual screens, teaching the emulator which colors to assign whenever that same tile is used elsewhere in the game.

Unfortunately, the re-coloring process doesn’t work perfectly in the current beta release. For one, the coloring algorithm seems to occasionally miss individual tiles, leading to some flickering, uncolored squares that stand out distractingly from their surroundings.

For another, this coloring process doesn’t work on games like3-D TetrisorRed Alarmthat eschew tile-based graphics for a more 3D wire frame effect. For these, VBoy Color also offers an option that lets you apply new palettes or color gradients based on the apparent depth of each line, making it easier to discern the 3D effect (especially on a flat monitor).

Even in its early state, VBoy Color features some high-quality emulation (built off of previous emulators like VirtualBoyGo and Beetle VB) and useful features like full stereoscopic support on VR headsets or3D monitors. All in all, it’s nice to haveyetanotheremulatorthat goesbeyond accurate gameplaytoactually improveon the experience delivered by original hardware.

item.title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
item.description:
The decried trial was canceled last week before police seized vaccine doses.

Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades.

In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial’s lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau’s Council of Ministers “formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October.”

The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissauraided Bandim Health’s offices and seized vaccines. Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected.

Of the trial’s rejection, Stabell Benn wrote: “We regret the decision because we considered the study scientifically and ethically justified, but we respect the government’s authority to decide whether research may proceed in the country.”

The World Health Organization and many outside experts have sharply disagreed with Stabell Benn and her colleagues on the trial’s justifications and design. It has been widely decried as “unethical” because it would withhold the newborn dose of hepatitis B vaccine from half of the participants.

With the country’s high rates of chronic hepatitis B infections, this would put thousands of babies at risk of developing a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Experts have further said that there is no scientific justification for the study, given the vaccine’s long use and strong safety record.The WHO wrote in Februarythat the trial “posits hypothetical safety outcomes without sufficient credible evidence” to justify putting newborns at risk.

Outrage erupted over the trial after the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced in December that it had awarded an unsolicited grant of $1.6 million to Bandim Health, which Stabell Benn runs with her husband Peter Aaby. The researchers are known for pursuing studies on nonspecific harms from vaccines and have been lauded by anti-vaccine advocates, including US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. But Aaby and Stabell Benn’s scientific peers have been critical of the quality of their work; the researchers are currently under investigation by Danish authorities for alleged scientific misconduct in their previous studies.

Their hepatitis B vaccine trial was reportedly halted in January by Guinea-Bissau authorities. But outcry erupted again after a report that the US CDC, under Kennedy, had onceset another $1.6 million aside to fund the trialand intended to move forward with it.

Stabell Benn and colleagues havepublicly lamented their tie to Kennedy. They have also consistently argued that their hepatitis B study is not unethical because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccine doses to newborns. Therefore, newborns not given the vaccine in the trial wouldn’t have received it outside the trial anyway. The country—which experienced a coup in November 2025—plans to introduce a birth dose in 2028, but it lacks the resources and infrastructure to do so now.

Outside experts, including the WHO, point to ethical guidelines, such as the Declaration of Helsinki, which require trials to provide the “best proven intervention” to participants, regardless of the current standard in the location where the trial is conducted. For hepatitis B prevention, the best proven prevention would be the newborn dose of the vaccine, which is globally recommended to be given within the first 24 hours of life. As the WHO wrote explicitly: “Resource constraints cannot be used to justify withholding proven care in a research study involving people.”

Stabell Benn and colleagues appear impervious to this point. Ina LinkedIn post Wednesday, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Bandim Health researcher involved in the trial, blamed the backlash on the “Anglophone media” that “framed [the trial] as dangerous because there would be a control group that would have followed the current vaccine schedule” in Guinea-Bissau.

Schaltz-Buchholzer’s post went on to claim that the media controversy has led to distrust of the hepatitis B vaccine in Guinea-Bissau and fears that the vaccine would pose a danger to newborns vaccinated in the trial, which he referred to as the intervention group, writing:

In the Bissau-Guinean context, it was widely understood that this trial was dangerous for the intervention group. For instance, rumours spread on social media with an omnipresent desconfiança (mistrust) that this was actually a novel vaccine to be tested by the Americans. Based on the Anglophone media coverage framing the trial as dangerous, Bissau-Guinean influencers speculated that the reason to test the hepatitis B vaccine in Guinea-Bissau was that the vaccine is dangerous, and that Bissau-Guinean newborns are disposable.

In her email to Ars Technica, Stabell Benn declined to say what reasons Guinea-Bissau officials gave for why the trial was rejected or why their office was searched and vaccine doses were seized. Ars Technica could not immediately reach Guinea-Bissau officials for comment.

But local distrust of the researchers could have played a role in the rejection and police operation. Stabell Benn said police were directed to investigate the vaccine doses directly, saying:

In its communiqué, the Council of Ministers instructed the competent authorities to investigate the origin, acquisition, transport, storage and traceability of vaccines intended for the proposed study. The Judicial Police subsequently searched the Bandim Health Project premises on 19 October and sealed the fridge containing a batch of hepatitis B vaccines. The vaccines were intended for the proposed study. The study had not begun, and none of the vaccines had been administered. We cooperated with the authorities.

Stabell Benn said the trial will not proceed and that Bandim has no plans to move it to a different location. “The underlying scientific question remains important,” she said. “But any future proposal would have to arise from an appropriate local context and partnership and undergo all required scientific, ethical, and governmental reviews.”

item.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
item.description:
Meta will appeal a ruling imposing the largest fine Mark Zuckerberg has ever seen.

Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws.

The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an$18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this yearwith attorneys general in nearly all states.

In hisopinionWednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”

New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.

Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NW Unfair Practices Act.”

“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.

To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.

“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”

Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a$5 billion settlementthe company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP Newsreported.

But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.

“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.

In apress release, Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”

“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.

The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the VergehighlightedMeta’s third-quarter earningsreport, which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.

The excessive penalties come asMeta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy, and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.

“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”

Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.

In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”

The company also failed to notify users when apps misused their data, only flagging two of 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse, Mathew said. Following its investigation, Meta’s “decision was deliberately made to narrow Facebook’s internal definition of data misuse so that Facebook would not have to notify as many people due to the operational burden of doing so,” he wrote.

Additionally, Facebook continued knowingly profiting off of pages with misinformation and hate speech, Mathew wrote. Internal research found “substantial amounts of misleading, false, and possibly false political, health, and science content,” with Meta documenting a “greater concentration of false content in top performing advertising content than in top performing Facebook content.”

Rather than share that research, Meta buried it, while also deceiving users in dozens of other ways, including by misrepresenting that the average Facebook users gets “equal treatment” to celebrities and influencers. While Meta claimed everyone was treated the same, one class of users received warning to remove violating content before strikes were applied and frequently got harmful or sketchy content decisions overturned in cases where most users would not.

Hegde told AP News that she thinks as Meta and other company’s AI products grow more popular, it will be increasingly important for states to remain watchful and protect residents from unknown harms.

“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”

Torrez vowed to keep watch in New Mexico and to continue using the blueprint from the Meta case to enforce consumer protection laws and prevent tech giants’ misuse of data.

“This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,”Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people.”
